This shows one [[advantage]] of learning from a video. A beginner can see that they could go back over a [[difficult]] part as many times as they need.

title: The bus with a garden on its side
text: A picture of [[tall]] sunflowers covers the side of a city bus. The name of a garden centre [[appears]] below the flowers. As the bus moves through streets full of grey buildings, the yellow flowers are easy to [[spot]]. People who pass the bus on their way to work may remember the garden centre when they want to buy [[plants]].

title: A simple meal for one
text: An advert for a frozen meal shows a [[single]] plate and a fork on a small table. The food pack [[beside]] it says ‘Serves one’. The scene shows [[exactly]] how much food comes in the pack. A person who cooks only for themselves can see that they will have [[enough]] for dinner without food left over.

title: A new pair of glasses
text: At first, the bus numbers in the advert look like grey [[marks]]. Then a pair of glasses [[comes]] into view, and the numbers look [[clear]] through them. This lets viewers see the street as the person in the advert sees it. Someone who has trouble reading signs may think about getting their eyes [[checked]].

title: The bench that remembers Dad
text: An advert for a park shows a woman sitting on a [[bench]]. A close-up shows the words ‘For Dad, who [[loved]] this park’ on a small sign. The park is [[asking]] people to pay for new benches. Showing one with a name helps viewers see how a gift can give people a place to rest and help a family [[remember]] someone.

title: A cake for a small party
text: Two cakes [[appear]] in the bakery advert. One is [[tall]] and has many pieces. The other is small and has just four. Showing the two [[sizes]] side by side helps people choose. Someone [[planning]] a birthday tea with a few friends can see that they can buy a cake without having lots left over.

title: The clean boots at the front door
text: In a video for a door mat, a child comes home with [[mud]] on his boots. He [[wipes]] them on the mat, then walks across a white floor. The floor stays [[clean]]. This shows the job the mat can do. People who are tired of cleaning muddy [[floors]] may see a reason to buy it.

title: A desk that grows with you
text: A child [[draws]] at a low desk. In the next shot, the same child is [[older]], and the desk is too low for her. She turns a [[handle]] to make it higher. This shows why the desk might be useful for years. A parent can picture buying it [[once]] and changing it as their child grows.

title: The red umbrella in the crowd
text: People [[hurry]] past the camera with plain black umbrellas. A woman [[opens]] a red one, and her friend spots her at once. The advert uses the [[crowd]] to show how different the red umbrella looks. A shopper who wants something easy to find in a [[busy]] place may remember the red umbrella when they next need one.

title: Meet the person who made it
text: In an advert for a plate, the camera follows a [[worker]] as she [[shapes]] the soft clay with her hands. At the end, she writes her name on the [[bottom]]. This gives the plate a story. Someone choosing a [[present]] can imagine telling the person who gets it who made it and how.

title: The second ticket costs less
text: A zoo advert shows two friends at the [[gate]]. Above them, the line ‘Bring a friend for half price’ is [[printed]] in large letters. The photo helps readers [[picture]] who they could take with them. Two friends who think a day at the zoo costs too much might decide to go together and [[share]] the cost.

title: No trips to the post office
text: In an advert for a parcel service, a driver [[takes]] a box from someone at their front door. Behind the [[customer]], we can see two more boxes ready to go. The short scene shows that people can send parcels without [[leaving]] home. This may appeal to someone who has [[several]] heavy boxes to send and no car.

title: The picture on the cinema wall
text: A poster for a new film shows a boy at the [[bottom]] of a deep hole. Above him, we can see a thin line of [[light]]. The poster leaves out the rest of the story, so people have a [[question]] to think about. They may want to watch the film to find out how he [[gets]] out.

title: The electric car without an engine note
text: At a red light, the driver [[lowers]] her window and hears a conversation on the pavement. The advert leaves the voices in the [[mix]] as the car pulls away. By letting an ordinary sound remain [[audible]], it gives viewers a way to judge how quietly the car moves. For buyers who associate a strong engine with a loud one, the scene also invites them to see [[quietness]] as a sign of progress.

title: The café that sells a break
text: Even a short visit to the café looks like an [[escape]] from the working day. Outside the window, people pass in a [[blur]], while a close-up shows a customer slowly [[stirring]] her coffee. The two speeds make the café feel separate from the rush on the street. For someone who spends the day watching the clock, a few minutes there may seem [[worth]] paying for.

title: The coat with a price per wear
text: Instead of hiding the high price, the coat advert puts it next to a much smaller [[figure]] for each day of wear. The calculation [[assumes]] the buyer will keep the coat for several winters. This gives shoppers a reason to think [[beyond]] the price they pay at the till. Its appeal depends on whether they can [[imagine]] wearing the same coat for that long.

title: Who gets the hero shot?
text: Finishing last earns the most [[dramatic]] shot in this sports drink advert. The camera slows down as the runner [[crosses]] the line, and the music rises when her teammates come towards her. These choices give finishing the race the importance [[usually]] given to [[winning]] it. The brand can appeal to viewers who enjoy sport without seeing themselves as the fastest person on the team.

title: The bike that stayed out of frame
text: We hear the chain [[slip]], see a flash of road and watch a hand reach for a [[brake]]. The repair service keeps the bike itself out of sight until it is working again. By breaking the ride into details, the advert puts us in the rider’s position before [[revealing]] what went wrong. For regular cyclists, that familiar moment of worry gives the repair a value [[beyond]] its price.

title: The account with a visible monthly fee
text: How much will the account cost each month? The bank answers that question in its [[headline]], with the fee [[printed]] as large as the account name. Many readers expect [[charges]] to appear near the bottom in small print, so putting the figure first makes the offer look more open. Even if the fee is higher than a rival’s, customers who [[dislike]] surprises may value knowing what they will pay.

title: A room without a presenter
text: There is no voice telling us what to notice in the furniture advert. Instead, we hear a drawer [[slide]] shut and a chair scrape [[softly]] across the floor. These sounds turn attention towards the [[materials]] and the way the furniture moves. A viewer watching on a phone may begin to [[imagine]] what it would be like to handle the pieces in a shop.

title: The train pass beside the petrol receipt
text: Placed next to a petrol [[receipt]], the price of a weekly train pass looks easier to compare with the cost of driving. The advert invites [[commuters]] to treat travel as a regular expense they can review. Its comparison is [[persuasive]] because the receipt looks familiar, although it leaves out costs such as [[parking]] and the time it might take to reach the station.

title: The advert that borrows the evening news
text: A local market advert opens with a [[reporter]] outside a stall and a line of text that looks like a news headline. The familiar format gives an [[everyday]] event a sense of importance. Viewers who [[recognise]] the playful copy may enjoy the idea that the arrival of fresh strawberries deserves a report. The joke works because the subject is much [[smaller]] than the format suggests.

title: A running app that praises a slow day
text: You showed up’ appears after a runner finishes a short route at a gentle [[pace]]. The app could have [[drawn]] attention to the slow time, but the advert keeps that number out of the shot. By praising effort, it gives beginners a [[measure]] of success they can reach straight away. This may make the app feel more [[welcoming]] to people who have given up on exercise plans before.

title: Two claims on a detergent bottle
text: Works at 20°C’ appears in a large circle, while the number of washes is [[printed]] below it. The first claim [[appeals]] to shoppers who want to use less energy, while the second helps them work out how long the bottle will [[last]]. The order tells us which reason the brand expects people to notice first. Buyers who compare prices may still give more [[weight]] to the smaller figure.

title: The last bus home
text: By the time the cook leaves work, the restaurant is [[closing]] for the night. We see him [[board]] the bus just as the lights go out behind him. By choosing a worker at the end of a late shift, the company shows who benefits from the new [[timetable]]. The detail also gives the service a social value that a list of departure times would be [[unlikely]] to communicate.

title: An empty frame for the camera
text: On a camera poster, a blank [[rectangle]] sits between two photographs of the same street. One shows the street at [[dawn]] and the other after dark. The words ‘Your turn’ appear inside the empty space. By leaving part of the poster [[unfinished]], the brand invites photographers to [[imagine]] adding their own view. The camera becomes a tool for finding a picture that the advert has left open.

title: The washing machine with the open door
text: A washing machine advert makes ease of use visible through the way its door opens. The person [[loading]] it is already holding a basket and pushes the door with one [[elbow]]. Keeping both [[actions]] in the same shot lets viewers see how the design fits a real task. Someone with a small laundry room may pay more [[attention]] to that moment than to a list of settings.

title: The label under the green leaf
text: A leaf takes up most of a drinks label, while ‘bottle made with [[recycled]] plastic’ appears in smaller letters. The image can create a broad [[impression]] that the product is good for the environment before shoppers read the words. The words themselves make a much [[narrower]] claim about the bottle. The gap matters because buyers may [[remember]] the leaf long after they have forgotten what the company actually promised.

title: The family photo behind the recipe
text: In an advert for a cooking kit, a teenager follows a [[recipe]] while an old family photograph stands on the shelf. The photograph makes a link between the new kit and the sort of cooking [[passed]] down at home. It may [[reassure]] buyers who worry that using a kit will feel less personal. The [[ingredients]] arrive in a box, but the meal can still feel like something they made for their family.

title: The password advert with a locked gate
text: Every time a character [[chooses]] an easy password, another gap appears in the garden gate. The sight of a child slipping through makes the weakness [[immediately]] clear. By comparing a password to a familiar kind of [[barrier]], the advert gives viewers a way to think about a problem they cannot see. The playful scene makes the warning easier to [[remember]] without making the risk seem far away.

title: The fan who refuses to change shirts
text: A football shirt advert follows a [[supporter]] through rain, defeat and an almost empty stadium. The shirt becomes [[easier]] to recognise as the crowd grows smaller. This choice presents [[loyalty]] as something that matters most when the team is [[struggling]]. Existing supporters may feel that the advert recognises their experience, giving them a reason to wear the shirt even when there is little to celebrate.

title: One wheel on the white line
text: In a tyre advert, the camera follows one wheel as it [[passes]] from dry road to standing water. There is no cut at the point where the road [[surface]] changes. That [[continuous]] shot makes the demonstration easier to follow because viewers can watch the same wheel through both [[conditions]]. For cautious drivers, the visible change in the road may carry more weight than a general promise of good grip.

title: The reminder that arrives at six
text: At six in the evening, a food app [[sends]] the message ‘Still time for a home-cooked dinner’. The wording matters because it suggests there is a [[choice]] left to make at the end of a busy day. Timing gives the message much of its [[force]]. Someone who would [[ignore]] the same advert after breakfast may open it when they are tired and have yet to decide what to eat.

title: The kettle with an old-fashioned click
text: Although the kettle can be [[controlled]] through a phone, its advert ends on the [[click]] of a switch. That small sound [[belongs]] to a familiar kitchen routine and makes the new feature feel less of a change. People who enjoy new devices can notice the phone control, while buyers who want a [[straightforward]] kettle still have something to recognise in the final shot.

title: The poster that puts a pupil at eye level
text: In a poster for a homework club, the camera is [[level]] with the pupil at her desk. We see the work [[spread]] in front of her and the empty chair beside her, where a volunteer could sit. That angle makes the appeal feel like an invitation to work [[alongside]] someone. Adults who worry they lack teaching [[experience]] may find this quiet scene easier to imagine joining.

title: The hotel room at ten in the morning
text: The hotel advert begins after a guest has already [[unpacked]] and starts work at the desk. Natural light comes through the window, and the camera shows [[space]] for a laptop and papers. Giving a morning of work this much attention changes who the room [[seems]] to be for. A guest who needs to work while [[travelling]] may value details that a usual picture of a neatly made bed would miss.

title: Four versions of the same chorus
text: A headphone advert plays one [[chorus]] four times as different people take turns choosing the sound settings. The drums become [[clearer]] for one listener, while another brings the voice forward. Repeating the same music gives the audience a fair way to [[hear]] the differences. The headphones can then appeal to people with different [[tastes]] without the advert having to present one setting as the best.

title: The bakery that shows its mistakes
text: A bakery video leaves in the moment a baker [[drops]] a tray of rolls and laughs. Keeping that shot changes the [[tone]] of the advert. The baker seems like someone we could meet in the shop, and the [[finished]] rolls feel less like objects made for the camera. This can build [[trust]] with viewers who prefer to know the people behind what they buy.

title: A billboard that changes with the weather
text: On dry days, the billboard shows a [[plain]] pavement. When it rains, a second image [[appears]] in which a pair of boots stands in the same spot. The wet weather becomes part of the [[demonstration]]. People passing the board are [[dealing]] with the conditions shown in the picture, so the message reaches them at a moment when they can imagine needing the product.

title: The phone in the kitchen drawer
text: An advert for a basic phone shows a teenager [[placing]] her usual phone in a drawer before dinner. She keeps the [[simpler]] device on the table in case someone needs to call. The scene gives being less connected a positive meaning by showing the [[conversation]] she can pay attention to. The offer may appeal to people who want fewer [[interruptions]] while still being available when it matters.

title: The missing finish on a desk
text: A desk advert places two close-ups side by side. On one, a [[scratch]] reveals a different colour [[beneath]] the surface. On the other, the wood looks the same all the way through. This comparison gives the customer a way to think about what happens after a desk leaves the shop. For someone who uses it [[daily]], the marks it will show may matter more than its [[appearance]] when new.

title: An advert that gets quieter as you watch
text: The longer the video runs, the more background sounds [[disappear]]. By the time the [[earplugs]] appear, all we hear is a clock in the next room. That slow change lets the audience [[experience]] the difference before learning what is being sold. It also gives viewers time to recognise the sounds they [[usually]] put up with, which makes the promise of a quieter room feel more personal.

title: The soup tin as a film star
text: In a soup advert, a [[spotlight]] falls on a tin as it turns [[slowly]] against a black background. The voice describes an ordinary lunch as if it were a major film [[release]]. That gap creates the joke. The brand can suggest that its soup deserves attention while showing that it understands how silly such a [[serious]] presentation would be for a quick meal.

title: The bookshop advert with two languages
text: On a bookshop window, the same welcome appears in two languages in letters of [[equal]] size. The books beside it include [[novels]] and children’s stories in both. Putting the languages on an equal [[footing]] shows that the second language is part of the shop’s everyday business. A family that reads in both languages may see the display as an invitation to [[browse]] together.

title: A pillow advert from the side
text: Rather than show a smiling [[sleeper]] from above, the pillow advert uses a side view. This makes it possible to see how the pillow [[fills]] the gap between the sleeper’s head and the [[mattress]]. The angle gives the viewer something [[specific]] to look for when choosing a pillow. That may persuade someone who has found words such as ‘soft’ and ‘firm’ hard to compare in a shop.

title: The fundraising total that moves
text: Every morning, volunteers [[update]] the number of tins on the food bank poster. The total goes up as [[donations]] come in, but the final target [[stays]] in the same place. This makes it possible to see both the progress made and the work left to do. Someone who can only give a few tins may see that their [[contribution]] still moves the total towards its goal.

title: The watch that belonged to someone else
text: Previous owner’ appears beside a photograph of a small mark on a [[second-hand]] watch. The seller could have [[cropped]] the image, but showing the mark makes its [[condition]] easier to judge. This choice also changes the way buyers might think about the mark itself. Someone who likes older objects may see it as part of the watch’s history, provided the seller is [[equally]] clear about how well it works.

title: A concert poster with a large letter
text: Most of the concert poster is taken up by one [[letter]] from the band’s name. Its shape [[matches]] the design on the band’s earlier album covers. Long-time fans can [[therefore]] recognise the poster from across the street before they can read the date. For someone new to the band, the same choice may give the poster a strong look while making it harder to tell who is [[playing]].

title: Tea at the speed of a timer
text: In a tea advert, the camera stays on the cup while the water [[slowly]] changes colour. A [[timer]] in the corner runs at normal speed, even though the screen shows only the last twenty seconds. The quiet wait makes the drink seem [[worth]] preparing with care. It may appeal to viewers who enjoy making tea as part of a daily [[routine]], even if it offers little to someone who values speed.

title: The review with one complaint
text: A shoe shop places a customer review [[beside]] a product photo. The review [[praises]] the shoes for long walks but says they took a week to feel [[comfortable]]. Keeping that detail makes the review sound more like an account of real use. A shopper might trust the praise more because the same customer has also given them a reason to think carefully about the [[purchase]].

title: Three seconds to find the message
text: Phone repairs upstairs’ takes up most of a poster beside an [[escalator]]. Next to the words, a photograph of a [[cracked]] screen shows the problem the shop can solve. People going past can take in the service and the direction at a [[glance]]. Someone on their way out of the shopping centre may decide it is worth going up a floor to ask about a [[repair]].

title: The chocolate bar after the credits
text: At the end of a short comedy, the actor stays in [[character]] and opens a chocolate bar. The packet sits in the same position as an object that caused trouble [[earlier]] in the film. That small reference [[rewards]] viewers who paid attention to the joke. It can make the product [[placement]] feel like part of the scene and help the packet stay in the audience’s memory.

title: The date hidden by a peel-off label
text: A music festival poster invites people to [[peel]] away a paper square to find the date [[underneath]]. Lifting the square gives a passer-by something to do with their hands, which may make the date easier to [[remember]]. The design still carries a cost. Someone who is [[hurrying]] past may notice the unusual poster and leave without finding the main piece of information.

title: The crisps behind the clear window
text: Through a clear [[strip]] in the packet, we can see crisps of different shapes and sizes. The advert shows the packet straight on, from the angle a shopper would [[normally]] see it. This makes the food seem less carefully [[arranged]] than it might in a picture of crisps in a bowl. Buyers can imagine [[checking]] the product for themselves before they pay for it.

title: The route chosen by a wheelchair user
text: A tourist board follows a wheelchair user who [[chooses]] where to stop on a day out. The camera shows the [[width]] of a doorway and the space between café tables as she goes by. Those details give the claim ‘Plan your own day’ a [[practical]] meaning. Viewers who need similar access can judge parts of the route for [[themselves]], and the person in the advert gets to direct the visit.

title: An empty shelf in a games shop
text: The advert shows one empty [[space]] on a shelf and adds the words ‘Back on Friday’. This can make the game seem [[popular]] before the shop gives any sales figures. It also gives people a date to remember. The idea relies on readers seeing the gap as a sign of [[demand]], although an empty shelf could also mean that the shop [[ordered]] very few copies.

title: A parcel that goes the other way
text: Most of the delivery advert follows a parcel being [[sent]] back after a customer opens it at home. The camera shows the returns [[label]] going on and the parcel being collected the next morning. By spending time on what happens after a purchase, the advert deals with a reason people [[hesitate]] to order. Buying online may feel easier if sending something back looks like an [[ordinary]] part of the service.

title: The price tag in a school uniform advert
text: A uniform advert shows the [[total]] price of a full set before listing the cost of each item. The order [[reflects]] the decision a family may need to make when several pieces have to be [[bought]] at once. If the shirt were shown first, the offer might look cheaper at a [[glance]]. Giving the total first makes it easier for parents to plan what they will spend.

title: A gardening advert set in winter
text: In a seed advert, a person [[brushes]] snow away from a garden step and sits down to draw a plan for spring. We see the seed [[packets]] only when she marks out what will grow where. The scene gives the product a [[purpose]] before it is time to plant. It may reach people who miss working [[outdoors]] and would enjoy having something to look forward to.

title: The handbag in a lift mirror
text: In a handbag advert, the product appears only in a lift [[mirror]] as people enter and leave. The camera stays on the reflection while coats and [[faces]] pass in front of it. This gives viewers a sense of how the bag looks when [[carried]] in a busy place. Someone who wants a smart bag for work can see how it fits into that [[setting]] without having to picture a different outfit.

title: The drink that changes its label
text: A juice brand puts different local place names on otherwise [[identical]] bottles. In the advert, friends [[search]] a shelf for the name of their town. The game gives shoppers a reason to look [[closely]] at a product they might usually pass. Seeing a familiar name can make an everyday [[purchase]] feel more personal, even though the drink inside each bottle is the same.

title: The pocket on the inside of the apron
text: A cooking advert hides the product’s main feature until flour [[spills]] across the worktop. The cook then takes a [[clean]] recipe card from an inside pocket. That small problem gives the feature a reason to [[appear]] at that point in the story. For home cooks who cover their phones or recipe books in flour, it makes the pocket easier to remember than a list of [[features]] would.

title: The advert you can read from a queue
text: A poster at a sports centre [[places]] a short question near the top and a longer answer at eye level. From the back of the [[queue]], visitors can read ‘What can I try for free?’ As they move closer, they can see the days and classes [[listed]] below. The layout matches the way people [[approach]] the poster and gives them a reason to read the details when they reach them.

title: Red letters for the sale
text: Big red letters [[spell]] ‘SALE’ in the shop window. The other words are [[small]] and black. People can read the red word from across the road. They know there are lower [[prices]] before they see the clothes. A person who wants a cheap shirt may [[cross]] the road to look inside.

title: Two ways to eat an egg
text: One side of the poster shows a cold egg on a [[plate]]. On the other side, an egg [[cooks]] in a hot pan. We see the butter [[move]] around it. The hot egg looks good to eat. The picture makes a person think about [[breakfast]] when they walk past the café.

title: The bus on the toy box
text: A toy bus sits [[inside]] a box with a clear front. Through the front, children can see the little [[seats]] and the driver. The picture on the back shows a child [[putting]] people on the bus. Now children can see what is in the box and how they can [[play]] with it.

title: The green arrow to the café
text: An arrow on the street points to the [[left]]. Under it, the sign [[says]] ‘Tea and cake’. People can read the sign while they walk. They know what they can buy and [[which]] way to go. Someone who wants to sit down for a cup of tea can find the café [[easily]].

title: Music for a dance class
text: The dance school’s video starts with a girl [[alone]] in a room. Then the music [[starts]], and three friends come in. They [[dance]] and laugh together. The music makes the class look like fun. A person who wants to meet [[new]] people may want to try the class with them.

title: A big bed for a small dog
text: In the shop’s advert, a small dog [[lies]] on a big blue bed. First it walks [[around]] the bed. Then it lies down and [[closes]] its eyes. The dog looks happy there. People with a dog can look at the picture and think about where their own dog likes to [[sleep]].

title: The number on the lemonade sign
text: £1 a cup’ is the [[biggest]] line on the sign. The word ‘Lemonade’ is just [[below]] it. People can see the price before they [[stop]] at the table. A child with one pound in their pocket can look at the sign and know they have enough [[money]] to buy a drink.

title: A hat in the wind
text: The boy runs along the [[beach]] in a red hat. The wind [[lifts]] the hat, but a string under his [[chin]] keeps it on. We can see why the string is there. A parent at the beach can look at the advert and think about how [[often]] a child loses a hat.

title: Five faces on a game poster
text: Five children sit on the [[floor]] in the picture. One child puts down a [[card]], and the others put up their hands. There is a big [[smile]] on every face. The smiles make the game look like fun. A child may want to bring the game to a party and play it with [[friends]].

title: A phone case on the floor
text: A phone [[falls]] from a table in the advert. We hear it [[hit]] the floor. The woman picks it up, and the [[screen]] still works. The picture shows what the case can do. People who drop their phones at home may see a [[reason]] to put a case on their own phone.

title: The bread shop’s first photo
text: Fresh bread [[fills]] the first picture on the bread shop’s website. We see a hand [[pull]] a warm roll open. The picture is close enough to show the [[soft]] bread inside. A person can almost feel the roll in their hands. They may want to [[visit]] the shop to buy one.

title: Two drinks with one ticket
text: On the poster, two cups of tea [[stand]] next to one ticket. The words say ‘Buy one tea. Get one [[free]].’ The picture makes it [[clear]] that two people can have a drink. Someone who sees the poster can think of a friend to ask. They may go to the café [[together]].

title: A light for the school bag
text: At the start of the advert, a girl looks in her bag after [[dark]]. She cannot find her [[keys]]. Then she [[turns]] on a little light in the bag and finds them. We see the problem and the answer. A student with a dark bag can see why the light is [[useful]].

title: A plate that goes in the bag
text: The yellow plate in the advert [[bends]] in a boy’s hands. He puts it in a small bag with his [[lunch]]. Later, he takes it [[out]] and puts it on the grass. The plate is [[flat]] again. The advert shows people how they can take a plate with them on a walk.

title: The ice on the fish
text: White [[ice]] sits under the fish in the shop’s window. The name of each fish is on a small [[card]]. The ice makes the fish look cold and [[fresh]]. People can look at the fish before they go in. A person who wants fish for [[dinner]] may stop and read the cards.

title: Three pictures for the pool
text: In the first picture, a child puts on a swimming [[cap]]. In the next, she [[walks]] to the water with her teacher. The last picture [[shows]] her in the pool. The pictures help new swimmers see what they will do at a [[lesson]]. This may make the first visit feel easier.

title: The long line for lunch
text: A photo on the wall shows a line of people [[outside]] a small food shop. The words under it say ‘Lunch [[starts]] at twelve’. The line makes the shop look [[popular]]. A person who has never eaten there may think the food is [[worth]] a try because so many people want to buy it.

title: A milk bottle for small hands
text: A young girl takes a small bottle of milk from the [[fridge]]. She [[pours]] milk into her glass with just [[one]] hand. No milk falls on the table. The advert shows why a small bottle is useful. Parents can see that a child can get a drink without [[asking]] for help.

title: The sign on the library door
text: Borrow books here’ is [[written]] in blue on the library door. Next to the words, a picture shows a bag [[full]] of books. The bag helps explain the idea. Children can take books home, read them and bring them [[back]]. This may make a child want to go in and [[choose]] a book.

title: A blanket on the grass
text: In the park, a family sits on a large [[blanket]]. The grass is [[wet]], but their clothes stay dry. When they [[stand]] up, we see water on the grass under the blanket. This shows why the blanket is useful. A family can plan a [[picnic]] even when it rains in the morning.

title: Two colours of school jumper
text: A shop [[shows]] a blue jumper and a green jumper side by side. The jumpers are the same [[size]] and the same price. Only the colour is [[different]]. The picture makes it easy to choose. A parent can look at both jumpers and [[pick]] the colour that the child needs for school.

title: A smile in the dentist’s window
text: There is a photo of a smiling girl in the dentist’s [[window]]. She sits in a big chair and [[holds]] a small mirror. The room looks [[light]] and warm. The picture can help a child see what the room is like. A first [[visit]] may feel easier after they see the photo.

title: The bell on the ice cream bike
text: In a short advert, we hear a [[bell]] before we see the ice cream bike. Children [[turn]] to look, and the bike comes into view. The sound helps us know when the bike is [[near]]. People who hear the same bell in the park may think about [[buying]] an ice cream.

title: The apple at the top
text: A red apple is at the [[top]] of the fruit shop’s poster. There are more apples in a box [[below]] it. The big apple is the [[first]] thing we see. It tells us what the shop has today. People who need [[fruit]] for lunch can decide to stop and buy some.

title: An empty chair by the door
text: A hairdresser puts a picture of an [[empty]] chair [[outside]] the door. The sign says ‘Come in now’. Together, the picture and the words tell people they do not have to [[wait]]. Someone with time before work can go in for a [[haircut]] without making a plan for another day.

title: A door with a clear number
text: The advert shows two front doors at [[night]]. It is hard to [[read]] the number on the first door. A small light makes the number on the [[second]] door easy to see. The two pictures show why the light is useful. A [[visitor]] can find the right house in the dark.

title: The towel in a small bag
text: A boy opens a bag no [[bigger]] than his hand. He takes out a [[towel]] and opens it on the [[sand]]. It is big enough for him to sit on. The advert shows that the towel is small in the bag and big on the beach. A person can [[carry]] it easily.

text: We [[hear]] a loud sound as a girl takes a [[bite]] of an apple. Then we see her eat the rest. The sound makes the apple seem [[fresh]]. People watching the advert can think about how a fresh apple [[sounds]] when they eat one. They may want an apple for a snack.

title: Three books for the train
text: The bookshop puts three [[thin]] books next to a picture of a train. A sign says ‘Short books for short [[trips]]’. The picture gives people an [[idea]] of when they can read the books. A person on the way to the [[station]] may pick up a book to read on the train.

title: The rug by the bed
text: In the advert, a girl gets out of bed on a cold [[morning]]. She puts one foot on the floor and [[pulls]] it back. Then she puts [[both]] feet on a rug and smiles. Her feet tell the story. People can see why a rug might make a cold room feel [[better]].

title: The shop with the yellow bags
text: Each person in the advert [[carries]] the same yellow shopping bag. One gets on a bus and another [[walks]] across a park. The shop’s [[name]] is on every bag. People see the yellow bag again and [[again]]. They may know which shop it comes from the next time they see one in town.

title: A first song on the piano
text: At the start of the piano advert, a boy plays just two [[notes]]. Later, he plays a short song and his sister [[sings]] with him. The two parts show a small [[change]] he can be happy about. A child who cannot play [[yet]] can see that a first song does not have to be hard.

title: A cup in one piece
text: In the poster, a [[broken]] cup is next to a box of [[glue]]. Below it, we see the cup in one [[piece]] again. It is easy to see what the glue is for. Someone with a broken plate or cup at home may stop and think about using glue to [[fix]] it.

title: The cake in the shop door
text: The bakery has a picture of a cake at the same [[height]] as a child’s face. The cake has a big smile [[made]] of fruit. Children can see the smile as they walk [[past]]. A child may stop to look and ask an [[adult]] to come in and see the real cake.

title: The jumper in the rain
text: A [[wet]] jumper hangs by the window in the evening. In the next shot, the sun is [[up]], and a boy puts the same jumper on for school. The words say ‘Wash it tonight. Wear it tomorrow.’ The two shots show how fast it [[dries]]. That may be useful to busy [[parents]].

title: Two children at the same desk
text: In a poster for an art club, two children [[draw]] at one desk. One draws a house. The other draws a blue cat with five [[legs]]. Both children have their pictures on the [[wall]]. The poster shows that there is room for [[different]] ideas. A child may want to bring their own ideas to the club.

title: A little fan on a hot bus
text: People on the bus are hot. A man [[wipes]] his face with his hand. Next to him, a girl takes a small fan out of her [[pocket]]. When she turns it [[on]], her hair moves. We can see what the fan does. People on the bus may want something that small to keep them [[cool]].

title: A new home for old toys
text: Pass it on’ is [[written]] on a box at a toy shop. A picture shows one child [[giving]] a toy train to another child. The two children look happy. The picture helps people see what [[happens]] to the toys they give. A family can [[bring]] an old toy and know another child can play with it.

title: The fruit in a clear cup
text: In a café advert, we see [[pieces]] of orange, apple and banana through the side of a cup. The café [[puts]] the cup next to the price. Customers can see what they get [[before]] they buy it. Someone who likes these fruits may choose the cup because they know what is [[inside]].

title: A key that is easy to find
text: A pile of silver keys [[lies]] on a table. One key has a bright [[pink]] ring. A hand [[reaches]] for that key at once. The colour shows why the ring is useful. People who spend time [[looking]] for the right key may want a bright ring for the one they use most.

title: A stamp on the museum map
text: The poster shows a child with a [[map]] and a stamp. There are three [[empty]] spaces on the map. The child [[puts]] a stamp in one space after seeing a big ship. The picture gives children a reason to look around the museum. They can find new things and [[fill]] in the map as they go.

title: The table at the birthday party
text: One photo [[shows]] a long table with no one around it. In the next photo, people [[sit]] at the table with hats and a cake. A café uses [[both]] photos in an advert. People can see how many [[friends]] can sit there and what a party might look like in that room.

title: The button under the picture of the cat
text: On a website, a photo shows a cat with its eyes [[closed]]. A small box [[below]] it says ‘See more cats’. A person looking for a pet knows what will happen when they [[press]] it. The website makes it easy to take one more step after a picture gets the person’s [[attention]].

title: The umbrella at the station door
text: Rain [[falls]] outside a train station. Inside the door, a sign with a blue [[umbrella]] says ‘Take one for £3’. The picture is easy to see near the door. People who left home [[without]] an umbrella may stop to buy one. They see the sign just before they go out into the [[rain]].

title: The photo on a bag of rice
text: At the [[front]] of the rice bag, the picture shows a bowl with rice, carrots and [[peas]]. A spoon is next to the bowl. The picture gives a shopper an [[idea]] for dinner. Someone who has vegetables at home may buy the rice because they can see a [[simple]] way to use it.

title: A chair that folds flat
text: Two people sit on chairs in a small garden. After lunch, one person [[folds]] both chairs and puts them by the [[wall]]. There is [[room]] for the children to play. The advert shows why chairs that fold are useful. A person with a small garden can [[use]] the same place for different things.

title: A green line around the park
text: A map on the poster has one green line [[around]] a park. It begins and [[ends]] at the same [[gate]]. The words say ‘Walk with us on Sunday’. The line makes the walk look easy to follow. Someone new to the park can see where to meet and where the walk will [[finish]].

title: The teacher in a video call
text: In an advert for English lessons, a teacher [[waves]] from a screen. A girl says one [[word]], and the teacher says it back slowly. We see the girl try again and [[smile]]. The advert shows what help looks like in a lesson. A new student can see that it is fine to try a word [[twice]].

title: The clock in the shoe shop
text: A sign in a shoe shop says ‘We [[close]] at eight on Fridays’. Next to the words is a picture of a clock. The [[hands]] show eight o’clock. People can see the time [[without]] reading every word. A person who works [[late]] may decide to look for shoes on the way home.

title: The blue cup at the bottom
text: An advert for a shop shows a long [[page]] of cups. Most of them are [[white]]. At the bottom, a blue cup [[sits]] next to the words ‘See all colours’. The blue cup makes people look at the words. Someone who wants a different colour can see [[where]] to look for more.

title: The discount that needs a friend
text: The poster [[promises]] half-price tickets if two people book together. Its photograph shows friends laughing on a train, making the [[condition]] feel like an opportunity to share a trip. The offer will be less useful to someone travelling [[alone]]. By placing the social scene beside the price, the company encourages readers to think of a companion before they [[question]] whether the ticket suits them.

title: A face hidden by the product
text: In the skincare advert, the model [[holds]] a bottle in front of part of her face. Viewers can see her smile but cannot study her skin [[closely]]. The unusual framing keeps attention on the product and creates a [[playful]] mood. It also means that the image offers little visual [[evidence]] for a claim about what the cream can do.

title: The advert that waits for silence
text: A radio advert starts with people [[talking]] over one another at a busy dinner table. The voices stop for two seconds before a single person [[asks]] for a hearing test. The [[sudden]] silence gives the question room to land. Listeners who have struggled to follow a conversation may [[recognise]] the problem before the service is named.

title: The cost shown in years
text: A company selling [[refillable]] pens [[divides]] the price by the number of years it expects each pen to last. The large final figure looks small, but it relies on the buyer [[continuing]] to use the same pen. This may persuade people tired of buying [[replacements]]. A careful reader will still want to know the price of the refills.

title: An empty bench in a crowded city
text: The park advert shows a [[packed]] street beside an empty bench under a tree. The two spaces are only a short walk [[apart]]. This [[contrast]] makes the park feel like an escape people can reach during an ordinary day. Office workers [[nearby]] may value the short distance as much as the view.

title: The jacket that returns next winter
text: The first shot shows a child [[wearing]] a winter jacket. The following year, a younger sibling wears the same one after a torn sleeve has been [[repaired]]. This short family story gives the repair service a [[practical]] value. It also suggests that looking after clothes can help more than one person, which may matter to families watching their [[spending]].

title: A train advert without a train
text: The poster shows a family [[already]] at the seaside, with wet feet and shoes in their hands. Only a small line at the bottom [[names]] the train route. By beginning at the [[destination]], the company asks viewers to picture what the journey would give them. People planning a day out may then [[search]] for the travel details.

title: The review beside the price
text: A customer’s comment appears [[directly]] below the cost of a camping stove. It says the stove was easy to use in strong wind but took [[longer]] than expected to heat water. Placing a mixed review beside the price lets shoppers weigh a benefit against a [[drawback]]. The balance may make the praise more [[believable]] than an advert offering only compliments.

title: A small word in a large claim
text: ‘Up to 50% off’ [[fills]] the shop window, but the words ‘up to’ are much [[smaller]] than the number. From across the street, shoppers may remember the half-price figure and miss its [[limit]]. The design draws them in, while the smaller words change what the promise actually means. A customer needs to [[check]] which items receive that discount.

title: The camera moves away from the star
text: A famous player opens the sports shoe video, but the camera soon follows the young [[fans]] who copy her practice [[routine]]. By giving them more time on screen, the advert makes the shoes feel [[relevant]] beyond professional sport. Her presence catches attention, while the later scenes [[suggest]] that ordinary players can take part in the same activity.

title: The museum poster with a borrowed voice
text: ‘I thought history was just dates’ is printed beside a photograph of a teenager [[holding]] an old sailor’s letter. The words suggest that the visit [[changed]] her mind. Teenagers who expect the museum to be [[dull]] may listen to someone their age. The letter gives that change a cause, rather than leaving it as an unsupported [[claim]].

title: A kitchen shown from a child’s height
text: The advert [[films]] a kitchen from low down as a child reaches for a glass. At this height, the shelves look far away, but the new [[cupboard]] opens within reach. The camera position lets adult viewers [[experience]] the problem before seeing the solution. Families may notice the value of a design they would overlook from [[standing]] height.

title: The advert with a slow clock
text: A clock [[ticks]] through a thirty-second video while a cook prepares dinner from a meal kit. The meal cannot [[actually]] be made in thirty seconds, and the advert does not claim it can. Instead, the ticking creates a feeling of [[progress]] as each step is shown. Busy viewers may remember the kit as a way to make dinner feel [[manageable]].

title: A label that carries the story
text: On the front of a bag of coffee, a short sentence [[names]] the farmer who grew it. The advert shows her [[checking]] plants before the beans are packed. Connecting a person to the [[finished]] product may make it easier to remember. Buyers interested in where food comes from may look for the name [[again]] in the shop.

title: The image that changes on a phone
text: The charity poster shows a street before and after new trees are [[planted]]. Online, viewers can [[slide]] between the two pictures with a finger. That action lets them control the [[comparison]] and notice changes at their own pace. Someone considering a donation can see a clear result the project hopes to [[achieve]], even though the image shows a plan.

title: A winter advert in bright sunlight
text: The coat company shows its new winter [[range]] on a warm day. Models [[carry]] the coats rather than wear them, and the words ‘Ready when it changes’ sit below. The unusual weather makes the advert less like a [[typical]] winter scene. It speaks to shoppers who prefer to prepare early, while giving them no chance to see the coats used in cold [[conditions]].

title: The lost glove on the train
text: A child leaves a glove on a train seat. Later, a staff member finds it and [[places]] it in a lost [[property]] box. The company uses a small object to show its care for [[passengers]] after the journey ends. Parents who have searched for missing things may recognise why this service matters, [[although]] the story does not promise that every glove will be found.

title: The same price in two cities
text: Two posters for a café show different streets, but the lunch [[price]] is identical. One street is busy with [[offices]] and the other is close to a school. Keeping the price [[constant]] gives the brand a clear message across both places. The photographs help each [[group]] of customers picture using the same offer in their own day.

title: The perfume that appears at the end
text: The video begins with a dancer moving through an [[empty]] theatre. We see light, fabric and [[movement]] for almost the whole advert, while the perfume bottle appears only in the final seconds. The [[delayed]] reveal gives the product a mood before viewers know its name. Someone who remembers the dance may [[connect]] that feeling with the bottle in a shop.

title: A food advert from inside the oven
text: The camera looks out [[through]] an oven door as someone places a tray of bread inside. Steam briefly [[covers]] the glass before the door opens again. This unusual view puts the audience close to the cooking [[process]]. People who enjoy baking may pay attention to that detail, even though the advertised product is the oven [[rather]] than the bread.

title: The ticket with an unfinished drawing
text: A festival ticket shows [[half]] of a bright picture. When two tickets are placed side by side, the drawing becomes [[complete]]. The design [[turns]] buying with a friend into a small game. It may encourage people to plan together, but a visitor going alone still needs clear information about the event [[beyond]] the playful image.

title: The word on the empty plate
text: ‘Enough?’ is written [[across]] an empty plate in a food charity poster. The question could be about the meal that has just ended, but the next line [[explains]] how many local families need help. Its brief opening makes people [[pause]] before the message becomes clear. The empty plate then gives the problem a simple, [[visible]] form.

title: An online shop that shows the queue
text: The [[checkout]] page tells customers that three people are looking at the same coat. This number may make the coat seem popular and create [[pressure]] to buy quickly. Someone who already likes it might [[complete]] the order sooner. The message gives no information about how many coats are in stock, so readers cannot tell whether waiting would [[actually]] matter.

title: A bicycle shown in parts
text: Instead of opening with a complete bicycle, the advert shows its [[brakes]], tyres and frame in separate close-ups. A rider then puts them to use on a steep [[street]]. The order asks viewers to notice how the parts work before [[admiring]] the finished bike. People comparing models may find these details more useful than a [[dramatic]] shot of speed.

title: The sound that returns at the end
text: The opening of a language school advert features a learner [[hesitating]] over a short greeting. Near the end, the same greeting [[returns]] during an easy conversation with a new friend. Hearing it twice makes [[progress]] clear without a test score. Viewers [[nervous]] about speaking may see that the school understands how difficult the first words can feel.

title: The restaurant with no food picture
text: The restaurant poster shows an empty table after a meal, with used plates and a [[note]] saying ‘See you next week’. This choice asks viewers to imagine customers [[wanting]] to return. It may be more [[memorable]] than another close-up of food, although someone choosing lunch for the first time still has little idea what the restaurant [[serves]].

title: The green roof from the bus
text: A bus company places its advert where passengers can see the roof of a nearby building [[covered]] with plants. The poster points to that roof and explains that the route stops [[beside]] its garden. Using something passengers can [[actually]] see makes the message easy to check. It also turns an ordinary [[journey]] into a possible visit.

title: The one word that changes
text: Two posters for a reading club show the same child with the same book. The first says ‘Read alone’, and the second [[replaces]] the last word with ‘together’. The small change draws [[attention]] to the club’s purpose. Children who already enjoy books may see that [[joining]] does not require them to change what they like, only [[where]] they share it.

title: A suitcase shown after landing
text: Most luggage adverts follow a person [[packing]]. This one begins at an airport after a flight, when the case [[rolls]] across a crowded floor and lifts onto a train. Showing the end of the journey gives the wheels and [[handle]] a reason to matter. Frequent travellers may judge a case by how it behaves when they are [[tired]].

title: The bakery with a public recipe
text: The bakery [[prints]] its bread recipe on the poster, including the [[amount]] of flour and the time it takes. Some viewers might wonder why a shop would tell customers how to make its product. For people who have tried [[baking]] at home, the long process may make buying a fresh loaf feel more [[appealing]].

title: A phone advert that shows a mistake
text: A teenager takes a photograph just as a friend [[closes]] her eyes. Instead of [[deleting]] it, they laugh and keep the picture. The advert presents the camera as part of a friendship rather than a tool for [[perfect]] images. Young viewers who enjoy taking casual photos may find this less distant than a carefully prepared [[portrait]].

title: The appeal that names a small goal
text: The charity poster asks for the cost of one school lunch and shows a [[tray]] with an empty space for it. The small [[amount]] may feel possible for someone who cannot give more. By focusing on a [[single]] meal, the appeal gives a large problem a clear first step, though the need will [[continue]] after that lunch.

title: A shirt that looks different in motion
text: The clothes website first shows a shirt on a still [[model]]. A short video below shows how the [[cloth]] moves as she reaches for a bag. The video [[answers]] a question the photograph cannot. Someone buying online may feel more [[confident]] about the fit after seeing the shirt in use.

title: The poster designed for a staircase
text: Each step up the station staircase [[reveals]] another line of a poster. At the bottom, travellers see ‘Going somewhere?’ By the top, they have read about a new weekend [[route]]. The placement matches the time it takes to [[climb]]. People rushing down the [[opposite]] way may see only part of the message, which limits who it reaches.

title: The clock that refuses to hurry
text: A watch advert shows a family cooking while its clock moves quietly in the [[corner]] of the screen. They take time to talk and [[finish]] the meal together. The watch is [[visible]], but the scene gives it a surprising message about time. It may appeal to people who want to use their hours well [[rather]] than fill them.

title: An old photograph with a new frame
text: The frame company places a faded family photograph [[inside]] a bright new frame. It does not [[change]] the picture itself. This helps viewers see that the product can give an old [[memory]] a place in the room today. People with photographs [[stored]] away may imagine displaying them instead of leaving them in a box.

title: The question below the star rating
text: A travel website shows a hotel’s five-star [[score]] beside the question ‘What mattered most to guests?’ Readers can open [[comments]] about the beds, breakfast or location. By [[inviting]] them past the number, the advert suggests that different travellers value different things. Someone with children may read about breakfast while a business visitor [[checks]] the desk.

title: The quiet customer in the busy shop
text: The camera follows a customer who stands [[silently]] while others ask for help. A shop worker [[notices]] her and comes over without waiting to be called. The advert presents service through a small action. People who dislike asking questions in busy shops may see the worker’s [[attention]] as a reason to [[visit]].

title: A shoe box that becomes a game
text: The back of the shoe box has [[lines]] for a simple board game. After opening it, a child and her friend [[use]] buttons as pieces. The advert gives the packaging a [[purpose]] after the shoes are taken out. Parents may see less waste, while children may remember a surprise that comes with the [[purchase]].

title: The camera placed at the doorway
text: An advert for a home alarm stays at the doorway while a family leaves. We watch someone check the [[lock]], then forget a small window. A light on the device [[signals]] that something needs attention. Keeping the camera [[still]] makes the oversight easy to notice. Homeowners may recognise how easily a detail can be missed during a busy [[departure]].

title: The bread that has to be shared
text: A large loaf takes up the [[centre]] of the bakery poster. Two hands reach towards it from opposite sides, and a knife [[rests]] nearby. The size and [[arrangement]] suggest that the bread belongs on a table with others. A person planning a meal with friends may think about bringing it home to [[share]].

title: The athlete who stops
text: In a sportswear advert, the runner stops [[halfway]] through training and sits on a wall. She drinks water, checks her [[breathing]] and then continues. Showing the pause gives the exercise a [[realistic]] rhythm. Viewers new to running may feel that they can begin without [[matching]] the pace usually shown in adverts.

title: A screen with one unanswered message
text: The phone company’s poster shows an [[unread]] message saying ‘Are you home yet?’ Its sender is [[marked]] ‘Dad’. A second picture shows the reply going through in a place with [[poor]] signal. The personal question gives the service a reason to matter. Viewers may think about who worries when they cannot be [[reached]].

title: The market advert made of receipts
text: Old shopping receipts [[form]] the background of a market poster. Over them, a large price lists what a [[basket]] of vegetables costs today. The design invites shoppers to [[compare]] the new price with what they have paid before. Its claim will only [[persuade]] them if the basket contains things they actually want to buy.

title: The blue dress in an ordinary room
text: A fashion advert [[photographs]] a bright dress in a simple kitchen rather than at a party. The model [[pours]] tea and reaches for a cup while wearing it. These actions show how it moves during an [[ordinary]] day. Someone who likes the dress but [[rarely]] attends formal events may picture getting more use from it.

title: The poster that makes the viewer wait
text: A poster has only the words ‘Wait for it’ and a picture of an [[empty]] stage. On the next street, a second poster [[reveals]] the date of a new play. Splitting the message can make curious walkers [[seek]] the answer. Anyone who sees only one poster, however, may leave without knowing what is being [[advertised]].

title: The warning inside a funny story
text: A road safety video follows a man [[searching]] everywhere for his car keys. The joke ends when he puts down his phone [[before]] driving. By making the audience laugh first, the advert may hold their [[attention]] long enough to deliver a serious message. The final action gives drivers something [[specific]] to do.

title: The same photo with two captions
text: A bank shows the same photograph of a student moving into a flat with two possible [[captions]]. One talks about [[independence]], and the other about paying rent on time. The picture can support both ideas. Presenting them together [[acknowledges]] the excitement and responsibility of moving out, which may speak to students more [[honestly]] than either caption alone.

title: A guide who stays in the background
text: In a museum video, a guide [[answers]] a child’s question and then steps [[aside]] while the child explores an exhibit. The guide is present without leading every moment. This may [[reassure]] parents who want help available while allowing children to make [[discoveries]] themselves. The balance becomes clearer through the guide’s movement than through a list of services.

title: The coat left on the train
text: A passenger gets off a train [[without]] her coat. The video follows a staff member finding it and taking it to lost property, then cuts to the passenger [[collecting]] it. The service is shown through a small everyday [[mistake]]. For travellers who often have their hands full, knowing what happens to lost things may make the company feel more [[dependable]].

title: The café table in two lights
text: The same café table is [[photographed]] in morning sunlight and under warm lamps at night. Nothing on the table changes [[except]] the food and the light. The paired scenes show that the café can [[suit]] different parts of the day. A visitor planning an evening meeting may notice the second image more than someone looking for [[breakfast]].

title: The countdown that starts again
text: An online advert says an offer ends in ten [[minutes]]. When a customer [[returns]] the next day, the same clock begins at ten minutes again. In the story, she notices and chooses to compare prices [[elsewhere]]. The advert is for a shopping advice service, which uses the repeated timer to show why people should check a claim before [[rushing]].

title: A photograph taken from the bus
text: A city tourism advert shows a famous square [[through]] a bus window. The glass catches a [[reflection]] of passengers, linking the [[landmark]] with the journey to it. The view suggests that visitors can see the city while [[travelling]] between places. Someone nervous about finding their way may value that sense of seeing the route.

title: The product that disappears
text: In a hair product advert, a bottle [[appears]] only while someone uses it. After that, the camera follows her through an ordinary day [[without]] showing the brand again. This gives viewers more time to look at the result than the [[packaging]]. It also asks them to [[connect]] her confidence with the product, even though other parts of her day may shape how she feels.

title: The empty chair in the team photo
text: A poster for a community team shows an [[empty]] chair at the edge of a group photo. The words ask for a volunteer to help with the team’s [[accounts]]. Leaving space for that person makes the role [[visible]]. Someone with those skills may see how they could [[contribute]] without needing to play the sport.

title: A discount beside a school bell
text: The snack shop’s advert plays as the school bell [[rings]] at the end of the day. A screen outside shows an [[offer]] for two drinks, and two friends stop to read it. The timing and the offer work together. Students who leave in [[pairs]] may decide to [[share]] the cost on their way home.

title: The washing instructions in the picture
text: Instead of placing the washing [[instructions]] only on a label, the clothing advert shows a person [[cleaning]] a mark from the sleeve. The scene answers a question someone might have after buying. Parents choosing everyday clothes may value this [[demonstration]] because a garment that is easy to care for can be [[worn]] more often.

title: The second hand stops at noon
text: A town clock [[fills]] a poster for a lunchtime concert. Its second hand stops at twelve, just as a small image of [[musicians]] appears below. The clock [[links]] the event to a time people can remember. Office workers nearby may realise that the concert fits within the part of the day they already spend [[outside]].

title: The question on the mirror
text: ‘Who do you see?’ is [[written]] on a mirror in a photography studio advert. Different customers stand in front of it, but the words [[remain]] in the same place. The question turns the studio visit into a [[chance]] to think about how they want to appear. It may appeal to people who want more than a [[standard]] portrait.

title: A parcel shown at the point of return
text: Most of the delivery video follows a box [[arriving]] at a house. The last third shows the customer changing her [[mind]], closing the box and sending it back. This gives time to a part of online shopping that adverts often [[skip]]. People unsure about ordering clothes without trying them on may find the return process [[reassuring]].

title: The sound of a missing player
text: A radio advert begins with the sounds of a football game, then [[suddenly]] loses the goalkeeper’s voice. A teammate asks where he has [[gone]]. The advert for a local club uses the gap to [[announce]] that it needs new players. Listeners who enjoy football may hear an invitation in the [[unfinished]] match.

title: A garden poster with no green
text: The poster for a garden show is almost entirely brown. It shows [[soil]], a pair of hands and small seeds just [[below]] the surface. By leaving flowers out, it [[focuses]] on the work that comes before them. Gardeners may recognise that stage, while people hoping for a [[colourful]] display may need the words to understand the event.

title: The shop window that counts down to dawn
text: At night, a bakery window screen [[counts]] the hours until the first bread comes out of the [[oven]]. People passing after closing time can see when to [[return]]. The countdown turns a closed shop into an advert for the morning. It may make fresh bread feel like something [[worth]] planning to buy.

title: The hotel advert with an open suitcase
text: The hotel video shows a traveller opening a suitcase and finding a [[creased]] shirt. She [[hangs]] it near a small iron and gets ready for a meeting. This ordinary problem gives the room’s [[equipment]] a purpose. A business guest may care more about that useful detail than about a wide photograph of the [[lobby]].

title: A poster with a familiar mistake

text: Rain falls while two people wait under the [[roof]] of a bus stop. They stay [[dry]] as a bus comes down the road. The advert is for the new stop, and it shows why the roof [[matters]]. People who wait there every day may be happy to [[use]] it.

title: The boy with the blue balloon
text: On the party shop’s poster, a boy [[holds]] one blue balloon. Behind him are many other balloons in [[different]] colours. The single balloon helps people see its [[shape]], and the ones behind show the choice in the shop. A family [[planning]] a party may come in to choose colours.

title: The cat who can see outside
text: A cat [[sits]] on a new shelf by a window. It looks at birds in the garden while its owner reads [[below]]. The advert shows what the shelf [[gives]] the cat. People with a cat and a small home may like a place for it that does not take up the [[floor]].

title: The old photo and the new photo
text: A picture on a wall is [[bent]] and has a dark mark. A photo shop shows it again after making a clean [[copy]]. The [[people]] in the picture are easy to see now. Someone with an old family photo may want the shop to help them see the faces [[clearly]] again.

title: A banana in the bag
text: A boy [[opens]] his school bag after a long day. His banana is still in one piece [[inside]] a little box. The advert shows the box doing one simple [[job]]. A parent who puts fruit in a school bag may like a way to keep it from getting [[hurt]].

title: The little path to the beach
text: A hotel poster shows a short [[path]] from a room to the beach. A guest walks [[along]] it with a towel. The picture makes it easy to see how [[close]] the water is. A family that wants to swim every day may like [[staying]] in a room near the sea.

title: The red sign for help
text: A red sign on a website says ‘Need help?’ in large [[letters]]. Under it, there is a picture of a person with a [[headset]]. People who cannot find an answer know where to [[press]]. The face also shows that a person can help them. This may make the website [[easier]] to use.

title: The first bite of a sandwich
text: In a food advert, a woman [[opens]] a paper bag on the train. She takes a [[bite]] of her sandwich and looks out of the window. Other people sit with [[empty]] hands. The scene makes the sandwich look like a good thing to take on a [[journey]], especially when it is time for lunch.

title: The green bag for old clothes
text: A green bag [[hangs]] on the door in a poster. An old shirt and a pair of shoes are [[inside]] it. The words say ‘Bring your old [[clothes]] here’. The picture shows what can go in the bag. Someone cleaning a room may [[remember]] the poster and bring clothes to the shop.

title: A yellow cup in a sea of blue
text: The advert shows many blue cups on a [[table]]. One cup in the [[middle]] is bright yellow. People look at the yellow cup first because it is [[different]]. The shop wants people to [[notice]] this colour. A shopper who likes bright things may ask where to find it.

title: The umbrella that covers two
text: Two friends walk in the rain [[under]] one large umbrella. They both stay [[dry]], and there is still room for their bags. This shows the [[size]] of the umbrella better than a number on a label. Someone who [[often]] walks with a friend may want to buy one this big.

title: The warm light in the window
text: It is [[dark]] outside a house, but a warm light [[shines]] in the window. The advert shows the same room with the light off and then on. The [[difference]] is easy to see. Someone [[choosing]] a lamp may think about how the light will make their own room feel.

title: A star for the reading club
text: A child puts a [[gold]] star next to her name after finishing a book. There are other stars on the reading club’s [[poster]]. The stars show that children can see how much they have [[read]]. Someone who likes [[collecting]] things may want to read another book and get one too.

title: The dog by the shop door
text: A dog [[waits]] outside a shop while its owner buys food. A little [[bowl]] of water is beside the door. The poster shows the bowl with the words ‘Water for dogs’. Dog owners may [[notice]] that their pets can have a drink. They may feel happy to [[stop]] at the shop.

title: The black shoes on a white floor
text: Black shoes stand on a [[white]] floor in the shop window. Nothing else is near them. This makes their [[shape]] easy to see. Someone walking past can look at the shoes [[without]] many other things taking their attention. They may stop to see the price or [[try]] them on.

title: A day at the farm
text: The farm’s website shows a child [[feeding]] a goat. [[Below]] the photo, a button says ‘Plan your visit’. The child’s smile makes the trip look [[fun]]. The button tells families what to do next if they want to go. They can look at times and [[prices]] on the next page.

title: The hot bread beside the clock
text: A [[clock]] on the bakery sign shows eight. Beside it, a picture shows hot bread coming out of an [[oven]]. The words say ‘Fresh at eight’. A person on the way to work can see when the bread is [[ready]]. They may walk past at that time to buy a warm [[loaf]].

title: A place for the wet shoes
text: A picture shows [[muddy]] shoes on a tray by the door. The floor [[beside]] the tray is clean. This tells people where to [[put]] shoes after a walk. Someone who is [[tired]] of dirt on the floor may want to buy a tray for their own front door.

title: The girl at the front of the class
text: A girl [[stands]] in front of a class and holds a [[drawing]]. The other children smile at it. The poster is for an art club, and it shows a child feeling [[happy]] with her work. Someone who likes drawing may want a place to [[show]] pictures to friends.

title: One red book on the shelf
text: Many grey books stand on a [[shelf]], but one book is red. The advert puts the red book in the middle. It is the [[first]] thing we see. People may remember the [[colour]] when they go to the shop. The picture helps them find the same book [[among]] many others.

title: A bowl that does not move
text: A dog [[eats]] from a bowl on the kitchen floor. It pushes the bowl with its [[nose]], but the bowl stays in the same place. We can see why this is [[useful]]. A dog owner who often finds water on the floor may want a bowl that stays [[still]].

title: The apple tree in the school yard
text: A poster shows children [[picking]] fruit from a tree in their school yard. There are red apples in their hands and on the [[ground]]. The words ask people to help [[plant]] more trees. The picture shows what a new tree could give children when it [[grows]] big and has fruit of its own.

title: A red bike with a bell
text: A small red bike is in the middle of the advert. A boy [[rings]] its bell before he rides [[past]] his friend. The [[sound]] makes the friend turn and smile. The advert lets children hear one part of the bike. They may want to [[try]] the bell at the shop.

title: The empty water bottle
text: The poster shows an [[empty]] bottle next to a tap. A hand holds the bottle [[under]] the water. The words say ‘[[Fill]] it here’. People at the sports centre can see where to get water. They may use the tap before a game [[instead]] of buying a new drink.

title: A chair for the bus driver
text: A driver sits in a new seat at the [[front]] of a bus. We see him [[move]] the seat back to give his legs more [[room]]. The advert shows one way the bus company helps its drivers. Someone who drives all day can see why a seat like that [[matters]].

title: The jacket on the hook
text: A child comes in from the rain and hangs a wet jacket on a [[hook]]. Water [[falls]] onto a tray below. The poster shows [[both]] the hook and the tray. A family can see where wet clothes will go. They may want one [[near]] the door at home.

title: The child with the ticket
text: A boy holds a ticket as he stands [[outside]] a theatre. His father [[points]] to the big doors, and they walk in together. The poster shows what happens at the [[start]] of a visit. A child who has never been to the theatre may feel [[ready]] to go.

title: A card with a song
text: A woman [[opens]] a birthday card, and a [[short]] song plays. She laughs and shows it to her friend. The advert lets us [[hear]] the song and see how she feels. Someone buying a card may want one that does more than give the birthday person [[words]] to read.

title: The new path through the park
text: On a poster, a thin blue [[line]] goes from the park gate to the lake. The words say ‘New path now [[open]]’. People can see [[where]] the path goes. A visitor who wants to see the lake may come to the park and [[follow]] the line on the map.

title: The fruit box at the door
text: A box of fresh fruit sits [[outside]] a house. A child opens the front door and takes out a [[pear]]. The advert shows that the fruit [[comes]] to the house. A family that cannot visit the market each week may like having fresh fruit [[brought]] to their door every Friday.

title: The shoe with the open side
text: A shoe shop’s advert shows a child [[opening]] a wide side of a shoe. He puts his foot in [[without]] help and closes it again with one hand. The close picture makes the [[steps]] easy to see. Parents can imagine a child [[getting]] ready for school on their own each morning.

title: The dog in the car
text: A dog sits on a mat in the [[back]] of a car. After the [[journey]], the owner takes out the mat. The seat under it is [[clean]]. The advert shows why the mat matters. A person who takes a dog on walks may want to keep [[mud]] off the car seats.

title: The five minute lunch
text: A small clock [[appears]] next to a bowl of noodles. We see the water go in and the [[noodles]] come out ready to eat. The advert shows how little [[time]] the meal takes. Someone with a [[short]] break at work may think this lunch is easy to make.

title: The scarf with two sides
text: In the first picture, a woman wears a scarf with red [[flowers]] showing. In the second, she turns it [[over]], and we see blue stripes. The pictures show that one scarf has two [[different]] looks. A shopper may like being [[able]] to change it with different clothes at home.

title: A small box for a big gift
text: A child opens a small gift box and [[finds]] a card for a day at the zoo. The next picture shows her looking at a [[giraffe]]. The advert shows that the gift is a trip, even though the box is [[small]]. A parent may want to give a day out as a [[present]].

title: The child at the bakery window
text: A child [[points]] to a [[loaf]] shaped like a turtle in a bakery window. Her mother stops to look with her. The [[unusual]] shape makes them notice the bread. The advert shows that food can be fun to see before it is [[eaten]]. A family may go inside to buy one.

title: A bright bag on a grey day
text: The street in the advert is [[grey]], and everyone wears dark coats. One person [[carries]] a bright orange bag. It stands out in the [[crowd]]. People can find the bag with their eyes at once. Someone who likes colour may want to [[look]] for it in the shop.

title: The number on the birthday candle
text: A cake has one [[candle]] shaped like the number six. Behind it are candles with [[other]] numbers. The shop shows that families can [[choose]] the number they need. A parent planning a birthday can see what to buy. The picture also makes the cake look [[ready]] for a party.

title: The milk at the front of the fridge
text: The advert shows milk at the front of a fridge [[shelf]]. A date is [[written]] in large letters on the bottle. The family can read it [[without]] taking the bottle out. People who sometimes forget when food needs to be used may like a label they can see [[easily]].

title: A small sign for a big dog
text: A sign [[outside]] a pet shop shows a big dog next to a little dog. Both have new [[leads]] on. This tells owners that the shop has things for dogs of different [[sizes]]. Someone with a large dog may stop because they can see that the shop has [[thought]] of it.

title: The picture at the end of the lesson
text: A child [[starts]] a drawing with a small blue circle. At the end of the art lesson, the [[circle]] is the centre of a big flower. The advert shows the start and the [[finished]] picture. A beginner can see that a picture can [[grow]] from one simple shape on the page.

title: The orange boat on the lake
text: A poster for boat trips shows one [[orange]] boat on a blue lake. The boat is easy to [[find]] in the picture. People can see that a guide sits at the front and visitors sit [[behind]]. A family new to boat trips may feel better when they know where [[everyone]] goes.

title: A table for one near the window
text: A café photo shows one small table [[near]] a window. There is a [[book]] and a cup on it. The picture shows that people can visit [[alone]] and feel comfortable. Someone who wants a quiet place to read may [[choose]] this café, even without a friend to meet.
